blocks.text: You run several projects at once, and your tasks live in spreadsheets, chat threads and a few free apps that don't talk to each other. Deadlines slip when nobody can see who owns what, and that's a hard problem to fix when your tasks sit in so many places.

We wrote this guide to help you choose the **best project management software for small teams** without testing a dozen tools yourself. It gives you a ranked shortlist of seven tools, each judged by the same four checks, and you can use it in these ways:

items: Compare prices per person, and use our simple way to work out the monthly cost for your own headcount.
Read the pros and cons of each tool, along with a clear note on who should skip it.
Pick two or three tools that fit your team and start trialing them this week.

blocks.text: Good software can break a big project into smaller tasks and keep [milestones and deadlines in one place](https://niftypm.com/blog/personal-project-management-software/). Luckily, you don't have to sort through every option on your own, because we checked each tool in the same way.

sections.h2: How we picked these project management tools

blocks.text: If you lead a team of 10 to 200 people, you probably care about how fast your team can start using a tool, whether the price is fair and whether everyone can see who owns what. We built our checks around those needs, so each tool is judged on the things a team lead feels first.

Honestly, small teams rarely have time for a long rollout, so we looked for tools you can try this week and judge by Friday. A week of setup before anyone gets value costs you real time, which is why speed to start is one of our checks.
Why small teams need a different kind of tool

A small team often can't spare someone to run its project software full time, so a tool that's easy to use matters more. [Sonary's reviews](https://sonary.com/project-management) give two examples of why this matters.

items: Its pros and cons note that ClickUp can be difficult to master because the platform is so expansive.

blocks.text: That's why we pay close attention to how quickly a new person can find their tasks and understand the board. A simpler tool that your team opens every morning will do more for you than a bigger one they avoid.
The four checks we use for every tool
Each tool in this guide gets the same four checks, so you can compare them fairly without reading between the lines. We judge each one on the following points:

items: We look at whether a free tier exists and what it lets your team do before you pay.
We note the starting price per person each month, so you can work out the cost for your own headcount.
We check which ways you can look at work, such as a list, a board, a calendar or a timeline.
We note how quickly a new teammate can get started without a long training session.

blocks.text: Those four checks line up with the details that comparison pages show side by side.
Where our prices and pros and cons come from
We take prices from each vendor's own pricing page and pros and cons from published reviews. Prices change often, so please confirm the current number on the vendor's page before you buy.
Some independent review sites also explain how they work.
We hold Planwise to the same four checks and the same rules as every other tool on this list, and we don't give it a higher spot because it's ours.
What a good tool does for you

Project management software helps because it breaks a big project into smaller tasks. It also keeps your milestones and deadlines in one place, so you don't hunt through chat threads to find out what's due.

As [Nifty explains](https://niftypm.com/blog/personal-project-management-software/), projects usually have tasks that depend on each other, and the right software lets you map those links and track the whole process in one place. Nifty also notes that collaborative features keep everyone on the same page when you work with a team.
How to use this guide
Read each tool section with the same four checks in mind, and write down your own answers as you go. Here are the steps we suggest for getting the most from the list:

items: Pick two or three tools that look closest to how your team already works.
Multiply each tool's price per user by your headcount to see the monthly cost before you commit.
Start a free plan or trial for each one and move a single real project into it.
Ask two teammates to use each tool for a few days and tell you what felt confusing.
Choose the one your team opens without being reminded.
